stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Ines, a visiting birdwatcher, has just told her uncle Tomas that the swallows nesting in his barn are a nuisance and should be driven off.

TOMAS: A nuisance? Each of those birds eats hundreds of flies a day. Before they came, my cows were tormented from June to September. Drive the swallows off, and the flies will be back before summer ends. I would sooner lose the barn roof than lose those birds.
choices: Ines argues that the swallows in the barn are a nuisance and should be removed.
Tomas argues that the swallows are valuable because they keep flies away from his cows.
Tomas worries that the swallows nesting in the barn will soon damage its roof.
Tomas claims that swallows eat more flies than any other bird in the region.
explanation: The introduction tells you Tomas is answering Ines's complaint. In plain English, his lines say the swallows eat the flies that used to bother his cows, and the flies will come back if the birds leave. His last line, which says he would rather lose the roof than the birds, sums up that view: the swallows are worth keeping.

A.why: You summarized the other character. The introduction gives Ines's view, but the question is about Tomas's speech, and he argues against her.

C.why: You read 'I would sooner lose the barn roof' literally. Tomas isn't predicting damage. He is saying how much more he values the birds than the roof.

D.why: Tomas says each swallow eats hundreds of flies, but he never compares swallows with other birds. You added a claim the text doesn't make.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set in an English weaving town in 1830. A merchant has just told Hannah, a hand-loom weaver, that the new power looms will soon put her out of work.

HANNAH: Thy machines may weave faster, I grant thee. But can they make a cloth that holds its pattern after twenty washings? Ask the ladies who buy from me whether they would trade my linen for thine. Speed is a fine thing, sir, but it is not the same as quality.
choices: Hannah accepts that power looms will soon make hand weaving an outdated trade.
Hannah is unsure whether machine-made cloth keeps its pattern after many washings.
Hannah argues that her handwoven cloth is better made, even if machines are faster.
Hannah explains that her customers are wealthy women who buy linen from her.
explanation: Rewrite Hannah's lines in plain English: 'Your machines may be faster, I'll admit. But their cloth doesn't last the way mine does, and my customers know it. Being fast isn't the same as being good.' She grants the merchant's point about speed and then argues for the quality of her own work.

A.why: This is the merchant's claim from the introduction. Hannah grants only that the machines are faster. She doesn't agree that her trade is finished.

B.why: You took a rhetorical question literally. 'Can they make a cloth that holds its pattern?' isn't a real question. Hannah means that they can't.

D.why: Hannah mentions her customers only to support her point about quality. You picked a passing detail instead of the claim it supports.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a novel. A student has just called the speech of a coastal fishing village "bad English." Her professor responds.

"Bad? Listen to how the fishermen say 'I be mending' for work they do every day and 'I'm mending' for a single job. That is not carelessness, my dear. It marks a difference standard English cannot show in so few words. Their grammar is not broken; it is simply different from ours."
choices: The professor argues that the village speech follows consistent rules of its own.
The student argues that the village speech is a careless form of standard English.
The professor argues that standard English is less expressive than any dialect.
The professor notes that the fishermen mostly discuss mending their nets and boats.
explanation: The professor rejects the word 'bad' and gives an example: the fishermen use 'I be' and 'I'm' to mark two different meanings. His conclusion is in the last line: their grammar 'is not broken; it is simply different.' The dialect has its own system.

B.why: This is the student's view from the introduction, and it's the view the professor is arguing against. You matched the wrong speaker.

C.why: The professor says standard English can't make this one distinction as briefly. He never claims it is less expressive than every dialect.

D.why: 'Mending' appears only in the professor's example. You picked a detail from the illustration instead of the point it illustrates.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Two researchers are diving above a reef. Leo, a new assistant, has just surfaced to report that the coral below has turned white and must be dead.

DR. OKAFOR: White, yes, but not dead. Coral turns pale when warm water forces out the algae living inside it. If the water cools within a few weeks, those algae can return. Dead coral is soon covered with seaweed. Tell me, did you see any seaweed down there?
choices: Dr. Okafor argues that the white coral is dead and can no longer recover.
Dr. Okafor argues that the white coral is weakened but may still recover.
Dr. Okafor argues that the coral will certainly recover once the water cools.
Dr. Okafor is unsure whether any seaweed is growing on the reef below them.
explanation: Dr. Okafor's first words, 'White, yes, but not dead,' state her point. She explains that warm water has pushed the algae out of the coral and that they 'can return' if the water cools. Her closing question suggests Leo saw no seaweed, so the coral isn't dead yet.

A.why: This is Leo's view from the introduction, and Dr. Okafor corrects it. You took the other character's claim for hers.

C.why: You missed the hedges. Dr. Okafor says the algae 'can' return 'if' the water cools within weeks. That is a possibility, not a promise.

D.why: You took a rhetorical question literally. Dr. Okafor isn't asking because she doesn't know. She's leading Leo to see that there is no seaweed.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Ruth, a patient trying to improve her diet, has just proudly told her dietitian that she has cut every bit of fat from her meals.

DIETITIAN: Every bit? Then how is your body to absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K, which dissolve only in fat? The goal was never to eat no fat, Ruth. It was to choose it well: olive oil, nuts, and fish rather than fried food and pastry.
choices: The dietitian praises Ruth for removing all fat from her daily meals.
The dietitian lists four vitamins that the body absorbs only with fat.
The dietitian advises Ruth to choose healthier fats, not to avoid all fat.
The dietitian wonders how the body is able to absorb certain vitamins.
explanation: The dietitian says it directly: 'The goal was never to eat no fat... It was to choose it well.' The point about vitamins explains why cutting all fat is a mistake, and the list of foods shows which fats to choose.

A.why: You took Ruth's pride from the introduction and gave it to the dietitian. The dietitian's 'Every bit?' questions Ruth's choice. It isn't praise.

B.why: This is true, but it covers only one sentence. The vitamins are the dietitian's reason, not her main point.

D.why: You took a rhetorical question literally. The dietitian knows how these vitamins are absorbed. Her question points out what Ruth's diet gets wrong.
